messages.subject: trouble optimizing a demo model
parts:
I put together a super simple multivariate Normal model,

data {
int<lower=1> N;
cov_matrix[N] ocov;
vector[N] omu;
real sampleSize;
}

parameters {
cov_matrix[N] ecov;
vector[N] emu;
}

model {
real det1;
matrix[N,N] Iecov;
real sum1;
vector[N] offset;
real fmean;

det1 <- log_determinant(ecov);
Iecov <- inverse_spd(ecov);
sum1 <- trace(Iecov * ocov);
offset <- emu - omu;
fmean <- quad_form(Iecov, offset);
increment_log_prob((sum1 + det1) * (sampleSize - 1) + fmean * sampleSize);
}

Data is attached. When I try to optimize this with,

./stan/src/models/openmx/mvn data file=stan/src/models/openmx/mvn.data.R optimize

Sometimes I get bad starting values where the expected cov_matrix is
non-positive definite. If the starting values are okay then the
optimizer always seems to give up on the first iteration. For example,

1 158.593 0 205.061 0.09193 0.001 77
Optimization terminated with error:

Line search failed to achieve a sufficient decrease, no more progress can be made

Suggestions?

I realize that this is a dumb way to sample the multivariate Normal. I
am actually interested in reusing the stan autodiff stuff for OpenMx,
http://openmx.psyc.virginia.edu/. I am building the model in stan
exactly the same way that the model exists in OpenMx so I can verify
that I get the same result in both softwares.

Thank you.

enough to help you here --- Marcus should be able to let you

optimizer in CmdStan 2.4.

The model as coded is going to be very difficult for
evaluation and autodiff arithmetically because you're directly
computing inverses. You might want to try the direct encoding
in Stan using sampling statements, which do the arithmetic a bit
more stably --- that might at least isolate the problem in the
arithmetic.

messages.subject: OpenMx and Stan
parts:
On Sat, Aug 02, 2014 at 12:28:22PM -0400, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > In OpenMx, multi_normal has two implementations. One implementation
> > handles data in the form of 1 case per row. The other implementation
> > handles data as a covariance matrix (and means). These two approaches
> > are equivalent for certain data (no missingness, etc).
>
> We don't have the latter in Stan, but now that you mention it,
> it seems like a good idea. Should be much faster to compute the
> stats on the data and then make a single call.

Yes, of course

If you're interested in further bridging the gap between Stan and
OpenMx, the next important feature would be RAM. Most OpenMx users don't
specify a model expected covariance matrix directly. Most OpenMx users
use the RAM specification (McArdle & McDonald, 1984).

In RAM, the covariance matrix is specified using an A and S matrix. The
A matrix gives the directional predictors (regressions) and the S matrix
gives the covariances. The benefit of this parameterization is that it
has a nice intuitive graphical interpretation. Some of my colleagues
developed a graphical, introductory SEM program,

http://onyx.brandmaier.de/

I'm not sure if Stan needs anything special to support RAM. The RAM
model expected covariance and mean vector are given by

\Sigma = F(I-A)^{-1} S(I-A)^T F^T
\mu = F(I-A)^{-1} m

where F is a filter matrix to select the manifest variables (hiding the
latent variables).

Can Stan already produce efficient derivatives for these expressions?

Since there are usually not long chains of regressions, there is a trick
to invert (I-A) very efficiently.

If this is easily accommodated in Stan then it would be a small step to
add "Export to Stan" functions in both Onyx and OpenMx. The vast
majority of SEM models are essentially multivariate Normal RAM models
(using either sufficient statistics or full information).

--

parts:
On Aug 2, 2014, at 10:20 PM, Joshua N Pritikin <jpri...@pobox.com> wrote:

> On Sat, Aug 02, 2014 at 12:28:22PM -0400, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>> In OpenMx, multi_normal has two implementations. One implementation
>>> handles data in the form of 1 case per row. The other implementation
>>> handles data as a covariance matrix (and means). These two approaches
>>> are equivalent for certain data (no missingness, etc).
>>
>> We don't have the latter in Stan, but now that you mention it,
>> it seems like a good idea. Should be much faster to compute the
>> stats on the data and then make a single call.
>
> Yes, of course
>
> If you're interested in further bridging the gap between Stan and
> OpenMx, the next important feature would be RAM. Most OpenMx users don't
> specify a model expected covariance matrix directly. Most OpenMx users
> use the RAM specification (McArdle & McDonald, 1984).
>
> In RAM, the covariance matrix is specified using an A and S matrix. The
> A matrix gives the directional predictors (regressions) and the S matrix
> gives the covariances. The benefit of this parameterization is that it
> has a nice intuitive graphical interpretation. Some of my colleagues
> developed a graphical, introductory SEM program,
>
> http://onyx.brandmaier.de/
>
> I'm not sure if Stan needs anything special to support RAM. The RAM
> model expected covariance and mean vector are given by
>
> \Sigma = F(I-A)^{-1} S(I-A)^T F^T
> \mu = F(I-A)^{-1} m
>
> where F is a filter matrix to select the manifest variables (hiding the
> latent variables).
>
> Can Stan already produce efficient derivatives for these expressions?

I'm assuming T is transpose.

The trick in getting efficient and numerically stable expressions is
to avoid inverse. So rather than directly evaluating F * (I - A)^{-1},
you'd evaluate F / (I - A), where matrix division is defined by

(X / Y) =def= X * Y^{-1}.

And yes, we can do these relatively efficiently. It'd be more efficient to
build in derivatives for the whole expression, but autodiffing with the
above shouldn't be a problem.

> Since there are usually not long chains of regressions, there is a trick
> to invert (I-A) very efficiently.

See above.

But if there's something more efficient we can do because I is known to
be an identity matrix, then we don't have that built in. Do you have
references on the trick required?

>
> If this is easily accommodated in Stan then it would be a small step to
> add "Export to Stan" functions in both Onyx and OpenMx. The vast
> majority of SEM models are essentially multivariate Normal RAM models
> (using either sufficient statistics or full information).
>

I don't even know what a "SEM model" is, but I assume other people
do. I saw some description of structural equation modeling in Sophia
Rabe-Hesketh's book on hierarchical models, but I didn't really
understand the notation, though it seemed to be underlyingly a notation
for regression.

- Bob

On Sun, Aug 03, 2014 at 12:58:11PM -0400, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> On Aug 2, 2014, at 10:20 PM, Joshua N Pritikin <jpri...@pobox.com> wrote:
> > I'm not sure if Stan needs anything special to support RAM. The RAM
> > model expected covariance and mean vector are given by
> >
> > \Sigma = F(I-A)^{-1} S(I-A)^T F^T
> > \mu = F(I-A)^{-1} m
> >
> > where F is a filter matrix to select the manifest variables (hiding the
> > latent variables).
> >
> > Can Stan already produce efficient derivatives for these expressions?
>
> I'm assuming T is transpose.
Yes

> The trick in getting efficient and numerically stable expressions is
> to avoid inverse. So rather than directly evaluating F * (I - A)^{-1},
> you'd evaluate F / (I - A), where matrix division is defined by
>
> (X / Y) =def= X * Y^{-1}.
>
> And yes, we can do these relatively efficiently. It'd be more efficient to
> build in derivatives for the whole expression, but autodiffing with the
> above shouldn't be a problem.

OK, there is a paper on computing derivatives for this model,

http://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/s13428-013-0384-4

But it would be nice to have anything working and then worry about
efficiency later.

> > Since there are usually not long chains of regressions, there is a trick
> > to invert (I-A) very efficiently.
>
> See above.
>
> But if there's something more efficient we can do because I is known to
> be an identity matrix, then we don't have that built in. Do you have
> references on the trick required?

The idea is to find out how many terms of the Taylor expansion you need
for an exact solution.

To find out how many terms you need, you multiply A by itself until all
coefficents are zero. This usually happens within a few iterations
because RAM models rarely have regression loops. Then the Taylor
expansion is

(I + A)
I + (I + A) * A
I + (I + (I + A) * A) * A
etc.

Of course it is better to have working code first and optimize it later.

> > If this is easily accommodated in Stan then it would be a small step to
> > add "Export to Stan" functions in both Onyx and OpenMx. The vast
> > majority of SEM models are essentially multivariate Normal RAM models
> > (using either sufficient statistics or full information).
>
> I don't even know what a "SEM model" is, but I assume other people
> do. I saw some description of structural equation modeling in Sophia
> Rabe-Hesketh's book on hierarchical models, but I didn't really
> understand the notation, though it seemed to be underlyingly a notation
> for regression.

I agree that the terminology can be a barrier. SEM usually means
multivariate Normal. There are two popular parameterizations of the
multivariate Normal, RAM and LISREL. In Stan, you have embraced so many
diverse distributions, it may be difficult to imagine that an entire
academic field is devoted to just one of them.
